strengths: Compelling mechanistic interpretability perspective: The paper provides interesting insights into how and where typographic information is processed in CLIP vision encoders, identifying that typographic signals emerge sharply in the second half of the network and are largely mediated by a sparse set of specialized attention heads.

Training-free and lightweight intervention: Defending against typographic attacks by simply ablating the CLS-directed residual updates of a small subset of heads during inference is computationally efficient and requires no gradient optimization or retraining.
Comprehensive scaling analysis: The authors demonstrate that this phenomenon holds across an extensive range of OpenCLIP model scales, from ViT-B up to the billion-parameter ViT-Big-G.

Causal validation: The paper validates the causal role of the identified circuit through controlled manipulation of the CLS attention sink (parameterized by alpha in Figure 5), confirming a direct link between head attention and typographic vulnerability.
weaknesses: Mathematical error in Equation 6: The definition of the Typographic Attention Score $T_{i,\ell}$ has $A^*_{i,\ell}(x)_t$ in both the numerator and denominator, which algebraically cancels out and reduces the summand to $1(t)$. The denominator was likely intended to be the sum over all spatial tokens $\sum_{t'} A^*_{i,\ell}(x)_{t'}$ or $\|A^*_{i,\ell}(x)\|_1$, and needs to be corrected.

Potential spatial bias confound in head identification: The Typographic Attention Score is calculated using Unsplash-Typo, where text is always placed at the bottom-center. Because ViTs frequently develop spatial/positional biases in attention heads, it is unclear whether the selected heads are truly specialized for text features or merely biased toward the bottom-center region. Evaluating text at multiple random locations during head scoring would ensure robust circuit identification.

Narrow baseline comparison and lower defense performance: The method is only compared against a single baseline (Defense-Prefix) and only on a single architecture (ViT-L). Other established defenses mentioned in related work (e.g., projection matrix learning by Materzynska et al. or weight-space patching by Ilharco et al.) are omitted. Furthermore, Defense-Prefix significantly outperforms the proposed method on typographic robustness (e.g., 82.78% vs. 65.00% on Disentangling, 71.82% vs. 69.09% on PAINT).

Scope limited to CLS-token consumers: Because the circuit ablation specifically zeros the head output to the CLS token ($H_{i,\ell}(x)_{cls} \mapsto 0$), spatial patch tokens still retain typographic information. Consequently, this defense does not readily transfer to modern vision-language models (e.g., LLaVA) or downstream vision pipelines that utilize patch tokens directly.

Drafting and proofreading issues: The paper contains several recurring typos and grammatical errors, such as 'behaivor' (pages 1, 9), 'casual' instead of 'causal' (page 9), inconsistent spelling of 'dyslexic' vs. 'dislexic' (pages 2, 7, 8, 9), and 'By suppresses' (Figure 1 caption).

strengths: Mechanistic interpretability approach to a well-known vulnerability: The paper provides clear, valuable insight into how CLIP vision encoders process text in images, showing that typographic information emerges sharply in the later layers and is driven by a small, specialized subset of attention heads.

Training-free and computationally efficient: Unlike existing defenses that require fine-tuning, prompt tuning, or auxiliary projections, the proposed circuit ablation requires zero gradient steps and operates directly at inference time.

Comprehensive cross-scale evaluation: The mechanistic findings and ablation strategy are evaluated systematically across multiple model sizes, from ViT-B up to ViT-BigG (billion-parameter scale), demonstrating that the phenomenon and circuit structure generalize across scales.

Causal validation: The controlled experiments manipulating the CLS-to-CLS attention sink weight (alpha) provide convincing evidence of a causal relationship between spatial attention in these specific heads and susceptibility to typographic attacks.

Minimal degradation on standard benchmarks: The method maintains zero-shot accuracy on non-adversarial benchmarks (ImageNet-100, Food-101, FGVC-Aircraft) within approximately 1% of the unablated models.
weaknesses: Limited baseline comparisons: The defense is compared against only a single prior method (Defense-Prefix). Other notable defenses mentioned in related work (e.g., weight patching from Ilharco et al., concept projection from Materzynska et al., or recent SAE-based steering) are not included in empirical comparisons.

Lower adversarial robustness compared to baseline: As shown in Table 4, Defense-Prefix significantly outperforms the proposed method on key typographic benchmarks, such as Disentangling (82.78% vs. 65.00%) and PAINT (71.82% vs. 69.09%). While the proposed method preserves non-typographic accuracy better, its defense against attacks is noticeably weaker.

Potential spatial confounding in score formulation: The Typographic Attention Score (Eq. 6) is derived from Unsplash-Typo where text is positioned strictly at the bottom-center. It is unclear whether high scores reflect true typographic selectivity or general spatial bias toward lower image regions.

Mathematical typo in Equation 6: In Eq. (6), the denominator appears to be written identically or inconsistently with respect to summation over spatial tokens ($A^*_{i,\ell}(x)_t$ in both numerator and denominator), which appears to be a typesetting mistake.

Greedy circuit search limitations: Algorithm 1 terminates immediately upon encountering the first head that causes $\Delta Acc \ge \epsilon$, which could be sensitive to ordering and might miss subsequent heads that are safe to remove, or ignore non-linear interactions among multiple ablated heads.

Limited applicability to modern Vision-Language Models: Because the ablation selectively zeroes out head outputs directed to the CLS token while leaving spatial token representations intact, the defense does not easily protect vision-language architectures (such as LLaVA) that consume spatial patch tokens directly.

strengths: Compelling mechanistic analysis: The paper provides clear empirical evidence (via layer-wise probing and intrinsic dimensionality analysis) showing that typographic understanding abruptly emerges in the later attention layers of CLIP's vision encoder, whereas general visual semantic features develop progressively.

Training-free and computationally lightweight intervention: Defending against typographic attacks by directly modifying attention residual updates at inference time requires no gradient optimization, making it scalable to large foundation models (up to ViT-Big-G) on modest hardware.
Extensive scaling analysis: Experiments and visualizations span multiple model sizes (ViT-B, L, H, G, Big-G), demonstrating consistent behavioral patterns across scales.

Causal validation: Section 6.2.1 and the attention sink manipulation (Figure 5) provide convincing evidence that the identified typographic heads causally drive the model's sensitivity to injected text.
weaknesses: Severe mathematical error in the core formulation: In Equation (6), the typographic attention score is written as $T_{i,\ell} = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}} \sum_{t \in \{1,\dots, T\}} \frac{\mathbf{1}(t) A^*_{i,\ell}(x)_t}{A^*_{i,\ell}(x)_t}$. The attention weight in the numerator and denominator trivially cancel out, leaving $\sum \mathbf{1}(t)$, which cannot be correct and appears to be an uncorrected typesetting error in the method's primary metric.

Limited defense efficacy compared to existing baselines: As shown in Table 4, the proposed method is notably outperformed by Defense-Prefix (DP) across typographic attack benchmarks (e.g., 65.00% vs. 82.78% on Disentangling). While the method is training-free, the performance gap on the target threat model is substantial.

Restricted baseline comparisons: The empirical evaluation only benchmarks against one external defense (Defense-Prefix on ViT-L), omitting other relevant existing defenses discussed in related work, such as weight patching / task arithmetic (Ilharco et al., 2022) or visual/text disentanglement projections (Materzynska et al., 2022).

Restricted scope due to CLS-only ablation: Modern vision-language systems (such as LLaVA, vision transformers in generative diffusion pipelines, and dense vision tasks) rely on spatial patch tokens rather than solely the CLS token. Because the intervention only suppresses the CLS residual update, typographic signals remain intact in spatial tokens, significantly limiting the defense's utility in modern multimodal architectures.

Lack of evaluation on intended text recognition / OCR tasks: The paper positions these models as 'dyslexic' drop-in replacements, but does not benchmark the trade-off on intentional visual text reading tasks (e.g., TextVQA or scene-text classification) to quantify how much useful reading capability is lost.

Noticeable typos and presentation polish issues: Several typographical errors are present throughout the text (e.g., 'Typograhic', 'behaivor', 'int the image', 'dislexic', 'casual' instead of 'causal', and 'cls tokent').

strengths: Compelling mechanistic motivation: The paper provides a clear interpretability-driven analysis showing that typographic information in CLIP emerges sharply in the latter layers and is transmitted to the [CLS] token via specific attention heads, supported by linear probing and intrinsic dimensionality analyses.

Gradient-free, zero-retraining defense: Unlike prior defenses that require expensive fine-tuning or token optimization (e.g., Defense-Prefix), Dyslexify operates via simple circuit ablation on the [CLS] residual stream, incurring zero training gradients and zero inference overhead.

Comprehensive scaling and causal validation: The authors demonstrate that the phenomenon holds across a wide spectrum of model scales (from ViT-B up to ViT-bigG). Furthermore, the causal intervention on attention sinks (Fig. 5) rigorously validates the role of these heads in vulnerability.

Diverse empirical benchmarks: Evaluations span multiple synthetic and real-world typographic datasets (RTA-100, Disentangling, PAINT), standard clean image benchmarks, optical character recognition tests (IIIT5K), and a safety-critical medical foundation model (WhyLesionCLIP).
weaknesses: Dismissal of adaptive attacks: The limitations section states that evaluating against adaptive attacks is 'not feasible' because typographic attacks are non-differentiable. However, attackers with knowledge of the ablated circuit could manipulate text placement, font styling, or use black-box/differentiable rendering techniques to route information through non-ablated pathways. A discussion or empirical check against varying font sizes, positions, or styles would strengthen the robustness claims.

Limited baseline comparisons: While the comparison to Defense-Prefix (DP) in Table 3 is informative, comparisons against other prior defenses mentioned in the related work (such as concept projection or weight interpolation/patching) are omitted.

Sensitivity to circuit construction hyperparameters: Algorithm 1 relies on hyperparameters such as tolerance epsilon, maximum consecutive skips k, and the choice of proxy datasets (D_img, D_typo). The paper lacks a sensitivity ablation showing how varying epsilon or using different text rendering styles in D_typo impacts the composition and generalization of the circuit.
Minor typographic errors in text: Several typos appear in the manuscript (e.g., 'Poject page' on page 1, 'gadient-free' on page 2, 'the the' on page 5, 'behaivor' on page 10).

strengths: Mechanistic interpretability approach to safety: The paper provides clear, insightful analysis into where and how typographic features emerge in CLIP vision transformers, showing that typographic understanding develops abruptly in the latter layers and is driven by a small circuit of specialized attention heads.

Completely gradient-free and computationally efficient: Unlike existing defenses that require fine-tuning, prompt tuning, or representation learning, Dyslexify modifies model behavior at inference time by zeroing head contributions to the CLS token residual stream, making it easily scalable up to billion-parameter models (ViT-bigG) without high VRAM requirements.

Convincing causal validation: The experiments in Section 5.2.1 and Figure 5 convincingly verify causality by manipulating the attention sink weight alpha, showing continuous and monotonic control over typographic vulnerability versus object recognition.

Broad evaluation across model scales and domains: The approach is validated across five OpenCLIP sizes (ViT-B, L, H, G, BigG) on multiple synthetic and real-world typographic benchmarks (RTA-100, Disentangling, PAINT), as well as a realistic safety-critical medical use case (WhyLesionCLIP for melanoma diagnosis).
weaknesses: Restricted to CLS-token-based architectures: The ablation specifically intervenes on the residual update of the CLS token (Hi,l,cls(z_cls) <- 0), leaving spatial patch tokens intact. Consequently, the defense cannot directly prevent typographic information from leaking into modern Vision-Language Models (e.g., LLaVA) or adapters that rely on spatial patch tokens rather than the CLS token.

Underperforms a simple preprocessing baseline: As shown in Appendix J (Table 9), a naive pipeline of running OCR (PaddleOCR) and applying a Gaussian blur over detected text regions consistently outperforms Dyslexify on attacked accuracy across all model sizes (e.g., 75.12% vs. 72.22% on ViT-L). While Dyslexify avoids inference-time compute overhead, this indicates that the circuit ablation leaves non-trivial typographic vulnerability intact.

Limited baseline comparisons: In the main paper, Dyslexify is compared only against Defense-Prefix (Azuma & Matsui, 2023) on a single architecture (ViT-L). Other relevant existing defenses mentioned in the literature, such as projection-matrix learning (Materzynska et al., 2022) or weight-space patching (Ilharco et al., 2022), are not quantitatively compared.

Trade-off with native OCR capability: By design, the defense degrades character and scene text recognition (as documented in Appendix H on IIIT5K, dropping 8-30% in word recognition accuracy). While acceptable for specialized zero-shot classification pipelines, this represents a significant capability sacrifice for general-purpose vision backbones.

strengths: Compelling mechanistic interpretability perspective: The paper successfully identifies and analyzes the localization of typographic processing within CLIP vision encoders, showing that typographic understanding emerges sharply in the latter layers and is transmitted into the [CLS] token by a small, sparse circuit of attention heads.

Gradient-free and computationally lightweight: Unlike prior defenses that require gradient-based optimization, prompt tuning, or weight fine-tuning (e.g., Defense-Prefix, model patching), Dyslexify requires zero backpropagation and introduces negligible computational/memory overhead during inference, scaling cleanly up to billion-parameter architectures (ViT-bigG).

Solid causal validation: The authors substantiate their mechanistic claims through controlled interventions (manipulating attention sink weights α), showing direct, monotonic control over the tradeoff between typographic and visual classification reliance.

Comprehensive evaluation across model scales and benchmarks: The method is validated across five OpenCLIP model sizes (ViT-B to ViT-bigG) on both synthetic benchmarks and real-world typographic datasets (RTA-100, Disentangling, PAINT), consistently showing substantial robustness improvements with minimal (<1%) drop in clean ImageNet-100 zero-shot accuracy.

Impactful real-world domain application: Demonstrating the vulnerability of medical vision-language models (WhyLesionCLIP) to typographic attacks and showing that Dyslexify recovers up to ~19% accuracy in melanoma classification provides practical motivation.
weaknesses: Restricted to [CLS]-token pooling architectures: Dyslexify operates specifically by ablating head contributions to the residual stream of the [CLS] token (H_{i,ℓ,cls} ← 0) while leaving spatial token interactions intact. As modern Vision-Language Models (e.g., LLaVA, Qwen-VL) typically extract dense spatial tokens rather than relying solely on the pooled [CLS] token, the current formulation cannot directly protect generative multimodal pipelines against typographic jailbreaks without substantial modifications.

Limited comparative baselines: The main experimental comparison is primarily conducted against a single method (Defense-Prefix) and only on ViT-L. Comparisons with other established defenses mentioned in related work (e.g., projection matrix approaches by Materzyńska et al., or weight patching by Ilharco et al.) are missing.

Synthetic supervision required for circuit identification: The discovery of typographic attention scores and circuit construction depends on synthetically generated typographic pairs (Unsplash/ImageNet-100-typo). The selection process relies on heuristic stopping criteria (ϵ, max skips k) and could be sensitive to the choice of font, text placement, or attack format used during localization.

Complete loss of OCR capability: As documented in Appendix H, ablating typographic circuits significantly diminishes the model's performance on legitimate text recognition benchmarks (e.g., drops of 10–30% on IIIT5K). This limits deployment strictly to environments where text reading is purely adversarial.

Preprocessing baseline outperformance: As noted in Appendix J, a naive OCR-detector followed by Gaussian blurring achieves higher absolute typographic robustness on ImageNet-100-Typo than Dyslexify across all models. While the authors reasonably argue about inference overhead and mechanistic value, this highlights that internal head ablation does not fully eliminate the vulnerability compared to external image sanitization.
